Agreed to run an expanded benchmark (5k prompts) and share a detailed cost spreadsheet. Suggested prefix caching + modest batching to hit latency SLOs while reducing unit cost.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-11
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~45m
Attendees: Sofia Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Cole (Redwood SE), Maria Lopez (CTO, Helios), James Wu (ML Eng), Priya Reddy (SRE)

[00:00] Sofia: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick agenda - cost/unit econ deep dive, bench updates, next steps. Maria, you good?
[00:18] Maria: Yep, thanks. We mainly want to see where we are on tokens per dollar and whether the caching changes you suggested actually move the needle.
[00:34] Ethan: Cool. quick recap - last week we enabled prefix caching on the H100 dedicated instance for the small subset and saw some KV hit improvement. initial numbers were noisy but promising.
[00:52] James: When you say noisy, is that because of the sample size or because requests vary a lot? We have a fat tail in token length.
[01:06] Ethan: both. sample size small; also we forgot to normalize for batching concurrency. a lot of short requests were batched together which inflated tokens/sec on paper.
[01:24] Priya: also our traffic has 20% long-form content, that skews average tokens per request.
[01:31] Sofia: right, so today we'll go through corrected tokens/sec/$ numbers for the last run, show caching delta, and discuss batching tradeoffs to keep 95th perc latency under 400ms.
[01:50] Ethan: ok, pulling up the spreadsheet. rough baseline: hosted endpoint with base model q4f32, with no caching and a concurrency of 8 gave ~12k tokens/sec per dollar on A100-class. with prefix caching enabled that moved to ~18k tokens/sec per dollar.
[02:15] James: 12k -> 18k, that is big. is that accounting for extra memory overhead?
[02:24] Ethan: memory bump negligible here; KV cache mostly lives in GPU memory but we tuned eviction. worst-case cold starts still hit full compute.
[02:35] Maria: can you explain tokens/sec per dollar calc? i want to ensure we're comparing apples to apples with our internal metrics.
[02:43] Sofia: yes - formula we used: tokens/sec observed * 3600 * 24 gives tokens/day, divided by hourly cost of the instance to get tokens per dollar. then normalized to 1M token units to compare to your billing. we include model variant price multiplier for dedicated.
[03:06] Priya: so does that include networking and storage costs?
[03:10] Ethan: no, that's compute-only. we can add a network adj but it's small for our workloads.
[03:17] James: what's the impact of batching? we saw better throughput but tail latency spiked.
[03:22] Ethan: exact - increasing batch size from 4 to 16 improved tokens/sec by ~30% but 95th latency went from 180ms to 520ms on the H100 config. prefix caching lets you keep smaller batches and still get benefit because it avoids redoing prefix compute.
[03:44] Maria: Any numbers for quantized models? we tried int8 earlier.
[03:49] Ethan: int8/4bit quant gave ~1.6x reduction in cost per token but introduced quality delta on a small subset of user prompts. also KV precision issues cropped up in one test (speech: "KV cash" in the raw notes).
[04:06] James: right our prod eval flagged hallucination regressing ~3% on the int8 run.
[04:12] Sofia: tradeoff conversation - for internal low-sensitivity features int8 might be ok to hit cost targets; for user-visible content we recommend q4f32 with caching.
[04:24] Priya: what's the dedicated vs hosted break-even? we're considering dedicated reserve for predictable throughput.
[04:30] Ethan: model dependent, but for sustained 24/7 traffic above ~6M tokens/day, dedicated with reserved capacity we modeled beats hosted. with caching included the break-even moves lower because you reduce GPU cycles.
[04:49] Maria: can you show the chart again that maps tokens/day to dollars for hosted vs dedicated?
[04:54] Ethan: yes - for our pilot dataset, hosted at current usage is about $0.40 per 1k tokens after discounts. dedicated amortized drops to ~ $0.22 per 1k tokens at 90% utilization. but that's sensitive to batch/concurrency and KV hit rate.
[05:15] James: what's realistic KV hit rate for our traffic?
[05:19] Ethan: with prefix caching and some request canonicalization, we saw 55-65% hit in the pilot. we think with small prompt normalization and sticky sessions you could push to 70%+.
[05:30] Priya: canonicalization means truncating certain metadata? we need to be careful with personalization tokens.
[05:35] Ethan: yes - strip variable trace IDs, normalize timestamps, keep user context tokenized consistently. we can give a transform script.
[05:46] Maria: about batching: is there an auto-batching policy to target latency SLOs?
[05:50] Sofia: Redwood has an autoscaler/batcher that can be configured to target percentile SLOs. you define acceptable 95th latency and it will pick batch windows and concurrency to optimize tokens/sec subject to that SLO.
[06:06] James: in the pilot we saw bursts where concurrency spiked and batching latency went through the roof. could be our request pattern.
[06:12] Ethan: two options: limit max batch size to cap latency, or use dynamic priority so interactive traffic bypasses large batches. both supported.
[06:22] Priya: do you have suggestions for initial config? our SLO is 400ms P95, target cost reduction 30%.
[06:29] Ethan: pragmatic starting config - enable prefix caching, cap batch size at 8, set concurrency target 6-8, aggressive KV eviction tuning for long sequences, and run a 5k-prompt benchmark to validate. that should get you into 20-30% lower unit cost while honoring 400ms P95 for most traffic mixes.
[06:52] Maria: that matches our goals. curious about the model fallback for capacity spikes.
[06:57] Sofia: we can route to cheaper model variants or to hosted fallback pool. Redwood's smart routing can fallback to a smaller quantized variant during high load while flagging quality. you control the policies.
[07:12] James: is the quality degradation visible in A/B? we need to monitor per-prompt evals.
[07:16] Ethan: yep - we integrate eval hooks to run your prompt set against both variants and track regressions. send us your eval set and we'll wire it into the POC.
[07:27] Priya: what's the approximate saving from prefix cache alone? you mentioned earlier 50%...
[07:31] Ethan: in our test sample prefix cache gave ~35-50% reduction in per-token compute depending on hit-rate. in your traffic with 60% hit we'd expect ~38% effective compute reduction. combine that with modest batching you can reach ~50% lower compute cost in favorable cases.
[07:52] Maria: any concerns on consistency or stale context when using KV cache?
[07:56] Ethan: stale context only if you reuse cache across different users; we namespace per session/user. eviction and TTL policies help. also we provide hooks to invalidate cache on content changes.
[08:10] James: ok on instrumentation - we need per-token cost breakdown and traces.
[08:14] Sofia: Redwood Console will give token-level cost and latency breakdowns, plus per-route dashboards. we'll share a demo link.
[08:22] Maria: earlier you said networking costs are small. for our media-heavy pipeline we might have embeddings and external calls - does that change the recommendation?
[08:30] Ethan: if you do heavy embedding or multimodal work, network / pre/post processing becomes more relevant and could favor dedicated to reduce egress; we'll add that into the spreadsheet when you share the sample.
[08:41] Priya: timeline - we want to decide on reserved capacity by end of March. can the expanded benchmark finish by mid-next-week?
[08:47] Sofia: yes, we'll run the 5k benchmark and share by 3/15.
[08:52] Ethan: action items recap - I'll run the benchmarks with cache on/off, and quantized variations, collect KV hit logs. Sofia will send cost sheet. Priya will upload the traffic sample.
[09:06] Maria: sounds good. one last Q - any immediate quick wins before the bench results? small config changes?
[09:13] Ethan: yes - enable prefix caching, apply canonicalization transform (we'll share script), and cap max batch size to 8. these are low-risk and should show improvement quickly.
[09:25] Sofia: ok let's recap next steps and owners.
[09:29] Maria: thank you all.
[09:31] Sofia: thanks, we'll follow up with links and the spreadsheet. bye.

End of transcript. Notes: occasional transcription artifacts ("KV cash"), speaker overlaps, and timestamps are approximate.
